questions.stem: Which statement best defines homeostasis in an organism?
options: Changing body temperature to match each change in the surroundings
Keeping each body variable fixed at exactly one value that never changes at all
Keeping a relatively constant internal environment despite external change
Keeping the internal environment identical to the external environment
questions.explanation: Homeostasis maintains internal conditions, such as temperature and water balance, within a narrow range. The values fluctuate slightly around a set point rather than staying perfectly fixed.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the stimulus-response model?
options: Stimulus, effector, receptor, response, control centre
Control centre, stimulus, receptor, response, effector
Stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector, response
Receptor, stimulus, effector, control centre, response
questions.explanation: A change (stimulus) is detected by a receptor, the control centre processes the information, and an effector such as a muscle or gland produces the response. The response then alters the original stimulus.

questions.stem: What makes a feedback loop negative feedback?
options: The response reduces or reverses the original change
The response makes the original change even larger still
The response happens only when the animal is unwell
The response is controlled without any receptors
questions.explanation: In negative feedback the response counteracts the stimulus, returning the variable towards its set point. A response that amplifies the change is positive feedback.

questions.stem: When a person's body temperature rises during exercise, the person sweats. In this stimulus-response pathway, what are the sweat glands?
options: The control centre
The stimulus
Effectors
Receptors
questions.explanation: Sweat glands carry out the response, so they are effectors. Thermoreceptors in the skin and hypothalamus detect the change, and the hypothalamus acts as the control centre.

questions.stem: A mammal's core temperature falls below its set point. Which sequence of events is negative feedback?
options: Thermoreceptors detect the fall, the hypothalamus signals, muscles shiver, temperature rises
Thermoreceptors detect the fall, the hypothalamus signals, sweat is released, temperature rises
Muscles shiver, thermoreceptors detect a rise, the hypothalamus signals, temperature falls again
The hypothalamus signals, skin vessels dilate, more heat is lost, temperature falls further
questions.explanation: Shivering generates heat and returns temperature towards the set point, which counteracts the original fall. Sweating and vasodilation increase heat loss, so they would make the fall worse.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an endotherm and an ectotherm?
options: Endotherms gain body heat mainly from the environment; ectotherms mainly from metabolism
Endotherms live only in cold places, while ectotherms live only in hot, dry places
Endotherms keep a constant temperature without needing to eat as much as ectotherms
Endotherms gain body heat mainly from metabolism; ectotherms mainly from the environment
questions.explanation: Endotherms such as mammals and birds generate most of their body heat from metabolism, while ectotherms such as reptiles rely mainly on external heat sources. Endotherms need far more food to fuel their high metabolic rate.

questions.stem: A bearded dragon lies on a warm rock in the morning sun and later moves into shade. Which type of thermoregulatory mechanism is this?
options: Metabolic
Behavioural
Structural
Physiological
questions.explanation: Moving between sun and shade is something the animal does, so it is a behavioural response. Ectotherms rely heavily on behaviour to keep body temperature within a workable range.

questions.stem: Which of these is a structural adaptation that reduces heat loss in a cold environment?
options: Shivering of the skeletal muscles
Huddling together in a group
Constriction of skin blood vessels
A thick layer of blubber under the skin
questions.explanation: Blubber is a feature of the body's structure that insulates against heat loss. Shivering and vasoconstriction are physiological responses, and huddling is behavioural.

questions.stem: On a hot day a red kangaroo licks its forearms, where blood vessels lie close to the skin. How does this cool the kangaroo?
options: Saliva reflects sunlight so that less heat is absorbed
Evaporating saliva removes heat from the blood near the skin
Saliva insulates the skin and stops heat entering the body
Licking lowers the kangaroo's metabolic rate to reduce its heat
questions.explanation: Water absorbs a lot of heat as it evaporates, so evaporating saliva cools the blood flowing close to the skin of the forearms. It is a behavioural response that uses evaporative cooling.

questions.stem: How does vasodilation of skin arterioles help a mammal cool down?
options: The blood vessels produce sweat, which cools the skin
The skin's metabolic rate drops, so it makes less heat
More blood flows near the skin surface, so more heat is lost
Less blood flows near the skin surface, so more heat is kept in
questions.explanation: Widened skin arterioles carry more warm blood close to the surface, where heat is lost by radiation, conduction and convection. Narrowing the vessels (vasoconstriction) does the opposite and conserves heat.

questions.stem: Arctic foxes have small ears and short legs, while desert foxes of a similar body mass have large ears and long legs. What is the best explanation?
options: Large extremities raise the surface area for losing heat in hot climates
Large extremities reduce the surface area for losing heat in hot climates
Small extremities allow more evaporation of water in cold climates
Small extremities increase metabolic heat production in the cold
questions.explanation: Large ears and long limbs increase surface area relative to volume, helping desert foxes lose heat. Small extremities reduce the surface area through which arctic foxes lose heat.

questions.stem: Which is a physiological response that increases heat production in a cold mammal?
options: Raising the metabolic rate, for example by shivering
Growing a thicker coat of fur over several weeks
Curling up into a ball to cover exposed body parts
Moving into a sheltered burrow out of the wind
questions.explanation: Shivering and an increased metabolic rate release more heat from cellular respiration. Curling up and sheltering are behavioural, and a thicker coat is a structural change.

questions.stem: In the legs of wading birds, arteries carrying warm blood lie next to veins returning cold blood from the feet. What is the advantage of this arrangement?
options: Heat passes from venous to arterial blood, so the feet are kept very much warmer
Blood mixes between the vessels, so the whole leg stays one temperature
Cold blood is sent directly to the heart, which lowers the metabolic rate
Heat passes from arterial to venous blood, so less heat is lost from the feet
questions.explanation: In countercurrent exchange, warm arterial blood heats the cold venous blood beside it, so heat returns to the body core instead of being lost through the feet. The arteries and veins remain separate; heat, not blood, is exchanged.

questions.stem: A lizard and a mouse of similar mass are kept at 10 °C and then at 30 °C. Which result is expected?
options: The lizard's body temperature changes with air temperature; the mouse's stays fairly constant
The mouse's body temperature changes with air temperature; the lizard's stays fairly constant
Both keep a constant body temperature, but the lizard uses more food to do so
Both body temperatures rise by 20 °C, because both are the same size
questions.explanation: The lizard is an ectotherm, so without behavioural options its temperature follows its surroundings. The mouse is an endotherm and uses metabolism and physiological responses to hold its temperature steady.

questions.stem: Why do ectotherms of a given size need much less food than endotherms of the same size?
options: They absorb most of their energy directly from sunlight on their skin
Their cells do not carry out cellular respiration to release energy
They store heat from food in their blood for many weeks at a time
They do not use energy from food to keep their body temperature high
questions.explanation: Endotherms spend a large share of their food energy on metabolic heat production. Ectotherms rely on external heat, so their metabolic rate and food needs are much lower; they still respire.

questions.stem: Which nitrogenous waste is most toxic and needs the most water to excrete?
options: Ammonia
Urea
Uric acid
Glucose
questions.explanation: Ammonia is highly toxic and must be diluted in large volumes of water, so it is excreted mainly by aquatic animals. Uric acid is the least toxic and needs very little water.

questions.stem: Most bony fish excrete their nitrogenous waste as ammonia. Why can they do this?
options: Ammonia takes the most energy to make, which fish can afford
Ammonia diffuses straight into the large volume of surrounding water
Ammonia is the least toxic waste, so it can be stored for long periods
Ammonia is insoluble, so it leaves the body as a dry paste
questions.explanation: Ammonia is very soluble and toxic, but in water it diffuses quickly across the gills and is diluted. Terrestrial animals lack that constant supply of water.

questions.stem: Birds and reptiles excrete uric acid. How does this relate to the availability of water?
options: Uric acid is insoluble and non-toxic, so it can be excreted with little water lost
Uric acid is very soluble, so it is flushed out with large volumes of water
Uric acid is the most toxic waste, so it must always be removed with lots of water
Uric acid is made without energy, so it saves water and energy together
questions.explanation: Uric acid can be excreted as a semi-solid paste, which conserves water in dry terrestrial environments. It is also safe to store inside a shelled egg. Making it costs more energy than making ammonia.

questions.stem: A frog tadpole excretes mainly ammonia, but the adult frog excretes mainly urea. Which explanation fits the change?
options: Urea is more toxic than ammonia, so only adults can tolerate it
The adult spends time on land, where water to dilute ammonia is limited
The adult lives in deeper water, where urea dissolves more easily
The tadpole has no kidneys, so it cannot produce any urea at all
questions.explanation: Aquatic tadpoles can lose toxic ammonia directly to the water, but adults on land need a less toxic waste that can be held in the body until water is available. Urea is less toxic than ammonia, not more.

questions.stem: Which correctly ranks nitrogenous wastes from least water needed to most water needed for excretion?
options: Uric acid, ammonia, urea
Uric acid, urea, ammonia
Ammonia, urea, uric acid
Urea, uric acid, ammonia
questions.explanation: Uric acid needs the least water because it is insoluble and low in toxicity, urea needs moderate amounts, and ammonia needs the most. Toxicity follows the same order.

questions.stem: A freshwater fish has body fluids with a higher solute concentration than the water around it. How does it maintain water balance?
options: It stops all water entering the body by making its gills fully waterproof
It produces large volumes of dilute urine and actively takes up salts at the gills
It drinks large amounts of water and excretes excess salt through its gills
It produces small volumes of very concentrated urine to save as much water as possible
questions.explanation: Water enters by osmosis, so the fish gets rid of it as copious dilute urine, while gill cells actively absorb the salts lost. Drinking and excreting salt at the gills is what marine bony fish do.

questions.stem: A marine bony fish has body fluids less concentrated than seawater. Which set of adaptations helps it maintain water balance?
options: It drinks seawater, stores all the salt in its body and makes no urine at all
It drinks seawater, excretes salt through its gills and makes little urine
It drinks no water, absorbs salt at its gills and makes lots of dilute urine
It drinks fresh water, retains salt in its tissues and makes lots of urine
questions.explanation: Marine bony fish lose water to the sea by osmosis, so they drink seawater, actively pump out the excess salt through gill cells and produce small amounts of urine. Absorbing salt and producing dilute urine is the freshwater strategy.

questions.stem: How do many seabirds, such as albatrosses, get rid of the excess salt they take in from seawater and food?
options: Their kidneys make large volumes of very dilute, watery urine
They store the salt as crystals in their feathers until moulting
They exchange salt for fresh water across their thin skin
Salt glands near the eyes secrete a concentrated salt solution
questions.explanation: Salt glands in the head excrete a solution more concentrated than seawater, which drips from the bill, so the birds can drink seawater and still gain water. Bird kidneys cannot make urine concentrated enough to do this alone.

questions.stem: Australian hopping mice live in deserts and may never drink. Which feature helps them conserve water?
options: They excrete their nitrogenous waste as ammonia
Their kidneys produce very concentrated urine
Their kidneys produce large volumes of dilute urine
They sweat heavily to keep cool during the day
questions.explanation: Hopping mice have kidneys that make extremely concentrated urine, so very little water is lost in excretion. They also stay in cool burrows by day and gain water from their food and metabolism.

questions.stem: Which of these is a behavioural adaptation that helps a desert mammal maintain water balance?
options: Producing highly concentrated urine in long kidney tubules
Releasing more antidiuretic hormone when blood is concentrated
Producing very dry faeces by reabsorbing water in the gut
Staying in a humid burrow during the day and feeding at night
questions.explanation: Being nocturnal and sheltering in a burrow is behaviour, and it reduces water lost through evaporation. Concentrating urine, releasing ADH and reabsorbing water from faeces are physiological adaptations.

questions.stem: When a mammal is dehydrated, more antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is released. What is the effect?
options: The kidneys stop filtering blood until water is available again
The kidneys reabsorb more water, producing less, more concentrated urine
The kidneys reabsorb less water, producing a larger volume of dilute urine
Sweat glands release more water to cool the dehydrated body
questions.explanation: ADH makes the collecting ducts more permeable to water, so more water returns to the blood and urine volume falls. This negative feedback response counteracts the dehydration.

questions.stem: What is metabolic water?
options: Water released by cellular respiration as food is broken down
Water absorbed through the skin from humid air in burrows
Water stored in the bladder for use when the animal is dry
Water taken in by drinking at a waterhole every night
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration produces water as well as carbon dioxide, and desert animals can meet much of their water needs this way. It does not come from drinking or absorption.

questions.stem: What is a xerophyte?
options: A plant adapted to survive in dry conditions
A plant adapted to survive in salty soils
A plant adapted to live submerged in water
A plant that grows only on other plants
questions.explanation: Xerophytes, such as many acacias and spinifex grasses, are adapted to environments with little available water. Plants adapted to salty soils are halophytes.

questions.stem: Many xerophytes have stomata sunken in pits and surrounded by hairs. How does this reduce water loss?
options: The hairs absorb the water vapour and carry it back down into the roots
The pits stop carbon dioxide from entering, so the stomata stay shut
The hairs make the leaf surface waxy and fully waterproof
Humid air is trapped near the stomata, reducing the water vapour gradient
questions.explanation: Still, moist air held in the pit and among the hairs lowers the difference in water vapour concentration between the leaf and the air, so less water diffuses out. Gas exchange still occurs through the stomata.

questions.stem: Which is a structural adaptation that reduces water loss in a xerophyte?
options: A thick, waxy cuticle on the leaves
Large, thin leaves with many stomata
Stomata open during the hottest hours
Short roots near the soil surface only
questions.explanation: A thick waxy cuticle is waterproof and reduces evaporation from the leaf surface. Large thin leaves with many stomata and stomata open in the heat would increase water loss.

questions.stem: Some succulent desert plants open their stomata at night and keep them closed during the day, storing carbon dioxide overnight. What is the main advantage?
options: Night opening lets oxygen in, so the plant needs no respiration
Gas exchange happens when it is cool, so far less water is lost
Photosynthesis happens at night, when there is the most light
Closed stomata by day let the plant take up salt from the soil
questions.explanation: Opening stomata in the cool night air greatly reduces transpiration while still letting carbon dioxide in; it is stored and used for photosynthesis in daylight. Photosynthesis needs light, so it still happens by day.

questions.stem: Many eucalypt leaves hang vertically. How does this help the tree in a hot, dry climate?
options: Rain runs off the leaves, so they never become waterlogged
The leaves catch more wind, which closes the stomata
Less leaf surface faces the midday sun, reducing heating and water loss
More leaf surface faces the midday sun, increasing photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Hanging leaves present their edges to the overhead midday sun, so they absorb less heat and lose less water. They still receive light in the morning and afternoon for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Why must xerophytes balance water conservation against gas exchange?
options: Water vapour must enter the stomata before carbon dioxide can leave the leaf
Closing the stomata stops water moving up the xylem to the roots
Gas exchange happens only through roots, which also absorb water
Stomata that let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis also let water vapour out
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide and water vapour diffuse through the same open stomata, so reducing water loss also limits carbon dioxide uptake. Xerophyte adaptations reduce water loss while still allowing enough gas exchange.

questions.stem: What is a halophyte?
options: A plant adapted to grow in cold climates
A plant adapted to grow in salty conditions
A plant adapted to grow in very dry sand
A plant adapted to grow in deep shade
questions.explanation: Halophytes, such as mangroves and samphires, tolerate high salt concentrations in soil or water. Dry-adapted plants are xerophytes.

questions.stem: Why is it hard for plants to take up water from salty soil?
options: The soil water has a high solute concentration, so less water enters roots by osmosis
The salt blocks the xylem vessels, so water cannot be pulled up the stem
Salty soil holds no water, because salt dries the soil out completely
Salt dissolves the root hairs, so the roots cannot absorb anything
questions.explanation: Water moves by osmosis towards the higher solute concentration, so salty soil water reduces or even reverses the flow into roots. Halophytes overcome this by keeping a higher solute concentration in their own cells.

questions.stem: Some mangroves have glands on their leaves that release salt crystals. What does this achieve?
options: Salt is moved from the leaves down into the roots for storage
Salt crystals attract water from the air into the leaves
Salt is converted into sugar for use in photosynthesis
Excess salt taken up with water is removed from the plant
questions.explanation: Salt glands actively excrete the salt that enters with water, so it does not build up to toxic levels in the leaf cells. Other mangroves exclude most salt at the roots instead.

questions.stem: Mangroves grow in waterlogged mud that contains very little oxygen. Which adaptation allows their roots to carry out gas exchange?
options: Thick cuticles: waxy layers that stop gases entering the roots
Pneumatophores: roots that grow up above the mud and take in air
Salt glands: leaf structures that release excess salt as crystals
Sunken stomata: leaf pores in pits that reduce water vapour loss
questions.explanation: Pneumatophores are aerial roots that rise above the mud and have pores through which air reaches the submerged roots. Salt glands deal with salt balance, not oxygen supply.

questions.stem: Samphire and other succulent halophytes store water in fleshy stems. How does this help them in salty soils?
options: The stored water dilutes the salt that builds up in their tissues
The stored water is pumped back out to wash salt from the soil
The fleshy stems stop all salt from entering the plant's roots
The fleshy stems take in salt from the air instead of the soil
questions.explanation: Succulence keeps the salt that accumulates in the cells at a lower, less damaging concentration. It does not stop salt entering or remove it from the soil.
